summary: The IMAP specification only lets a client search the selected mailbox. This extension lets a client search multiple mailboxes with a single command, avoiding repeated SELECT and SEARCH round trips and the delays they cause.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of opening each drawer in turn to find a letter, you ask once and every drawer is checked. This RFC lets email programs search many folders in one go.

questions: how to search all mailboxes in imap
what is the imap esearch command
subtitle: One IMAP command that searches many mailboxes at once, without disturbing the one you have open.

tldr.problem: Base IMAP can only search the selected mailbox, so a client that wants to search several must issue a series of SELECT and SEARCH commands and wait for each to finish.
tldr.mechanism: The ESEARCH command takes source options naming the mailboxes to search, and each ESEARCH response carries MAILBOX, UIDVALIDITY and TAG correlators so results can be told apart.
tldr.outcome: Clients save round trips and can pipeline searches. This Standards Track document obsoletes the earlier Experimental RFC 6237 and updates RFC 4466.

today: RFC 7377 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Experimental RFC 6237 and updates RFC 4466. The metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why One Search Is Not Enough
sections.content:
The IMAP4 specification allows searching only the selected mailbox. A user often wants to search several. A client that wants to do that must issue a series of SELECT and SEARCH commands, waiting for each to complete before moving on.

Those commands cannot be pipelined, because the server might run them in parallel and the untagged SEARCH responses could not then be told apart. This extension was previously published in an Experimental RFC. With implementation experience behind it, this document moves it to the Standards Track with minor updates.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine checking ten drawers one at a time, closing each before opening the next. It is slow, and if you ask about two drawers at once the answers get mixed up.

sections.title: The ESEARCH Command
sections.content:
The new ESEARCH command works like the UID SEARCH command, with optional source options and result options. Its arguments are optional source options, optional result options, an optional charset, and one or more searching criteria. The result is OK when the search completed, NO for an unsearchable charset or criteria, and BAD for an unknown command or invalid arguments.

A server that supports the extension includes MULTISEARCH in its IMAP capability string. This document defines no new result options.

A message range that extends beyond the end of the mailbox MUST NOT be treated as an error. A client can slide a window such as 1:100 then 101:200 and decide for itself when to stop.
sections.plainLanguage: ESEARCH is a new way of asking the mail server a question. You say which folders to look in and what you are looking for, and the server does the rest.

sections.title: The ESEARCH Response and Correlators
sections.content:
The server MUST answer with ESEARCH responses, not SEARCH responses. Message numbers are not useful for mailboxes that are not selected, so the responses MUST contain UIDs. If a source option is given without a result option, the ALL result option is implied.

For each mailbox that satisfies the source options, one ESEARCH response MUST be returned if any message matches, and none for mailboxes with no matches. Values from MIN, MAX and COUNT apply to the mailbox named in that response. A search with no matches anywhere returns only the tagged OK.

Every response MUST contain the MAILBOX, TAG and UIDVALIDITY correlators, which let a client issue several ESEARCH commands at once. If the SEARCHRES extension is used, that command MUST run after all previous SEARCH or ESEARCH commands finish and before any later ones start.
sections.plainLanguage: Each answer comes with a label saying which folder it came from and which question it answers. That way the answers can arrive in any order and still make sense.

sections.title: Choosing Which Mailboxes to Search
sections.content:
Source options use the mailbox specifiers from the IMAP NOTIFY extension (RFC 5465), with two differences: selected-delayed is not valid here, and a new subtree-one specifier is added. subtree searches a mailbox and all selectable mailboxes below it at any depth, while subtree-one goes only one level down.

  • If no source options are given, selected is assumed.
  • The personal option searches all of the user's mailboxes. Wildcards are not expanded by the mailboxes option.
  • With subtree, the server MUST defend against loops in the hierarchy, preferably by tracking mailboxes already searched, or else by limiting depth.
  • Searching selected requires the session to be in selected state. Otherwise selected or authenticated state is enough. A wrong state gets a BAD result.
  • Clients SHOULD NOT list the same mailbox twice, and a server MAY answer BAD if they do.

Extra rules apply when other extensions are present. The SEARCHRES SAVE option is valid only when selected is the sole mailbox. With the Contexts extension, UPDATE applies only to the selected mailbox. With the ACL extension, the user needs the r right on each mailbox and the l right on mailboxes not named explicitly, and mailboxes lacking those rights are silently ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: You can say 'just this folder', 'this folder and the ones inside it', or 'all my folders'. The server is careful not to go round in circles if folders link back to each other.

sections.title: Fuzzy Matching and Search Limits
sections.content:
The base IMAP SEARCH requires strict substring matching. Many servers use search engines that match differently, for example matching 'swim' to 'swam' and 'swum'. This extension is compatible with the Fuzzy Search extension (RFC 6203), and explicitly allows servers to use fuzzy matching for TEXT and BODY searches.

Servers MAY also limit search volume, such as the number of mailboxes or the number or total size of messages searched. A server can refuse up front with NO [LIMIT], or run the search and stop at the limit with OK [LIMIT] and partial results. The RFC warns that partial results can complicate clients and confuse users.
sections.plainLanguage: The server may guess that 'swim' and 'swam' mean about the same thing. It may also say 'that is too many folders for one go' so one person cannot hog the machine.

sections.title: A Pipelined Example
sections.content: The RFC's example sends two ESEARCH commands back to back. tag1 looks for unseen messages in folder1 and the subtree of folder2. tag2 searches folder1 and the one-level subtree of folder2 for subject 'chad'. The server runs them in parallel, and a tag2 response appears among the tag1 responses. The TAG, MAILBOX and UIDVALIDITY fields keep every result matched to its search.
sections.plainLanguage: Two people ask questions at once and the helper answers them mixed together. Name tags on every answer show who asked what.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
One command can now trigger an expensive search of tens of thousands of mailboxes, so servers need ways to stop a client from harming other users. Limits on the number of mailboxes or on the resources spent for one client are called reasonable.

Implementations MUST apply access controls as for any other IMAP command, and the extension has no data-access risks beyond unextended IMAP. Mailboxes the user lacks rights to are ignored, because telling insufficient access apart from nonexistence could expose the mailbox hierarchy. Servers MUST also defend against hierarchy loops when subtree is used. IANA changed the reference for the MULTISEARCH capability to point to this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A big question can make the server work very hard, so it may say no to huge ones. It also never hints at folders you are not allowed to see.

sections.title: Changes Since RFC 6237
sections.content: Compared with the Experimental RFC 6237, this document changes the status to Standards Track, adds a paragraph about duplicate mailboxes, and adds the section on Fuzzy Search. It also updates the search-correlator item from RFC 4466 by adding the MAILBOX and UIDVALIDITY fields.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the grown-up version of an earlier trial. It adds a rule about naming a folder twice and a note about fuzzy matching.

data.title: Pipelined ESEARCH
data.code:
C: tag1 ESEARCH IN (mailboxes "folder1" subtree "folder2") unseen
C: tag2 ESEARCH IN (mailboxes "folder1" subtree-one "folder2")
   subject "chad"
S: * ESEARCH (TAG "tag1" MAILBOX "folder1" UIDVALIDITY 1) UID ALL
   4001,4003,4005,4007,4009
S: * ESEARCH (TAG "tag2" MAILBOX "folder1" UIDVALIDITY 1) UID ALL
   3001:3004,3788
S: tag1 OK done
